The main argument is that brains are not computers. Seth says this is the first and most important of his four arguments [spya-a8jgf4].

Computers cleanly separate the software (the algorithm) from the hardware that runs it. Turing computation is built on that separation, so it can run on any suitable material [spya-dfujdu]. A brain has no such split. What it does and what it is can't be pulled apart, from single neurons up to whole-brain activity [spya-zw2m7u]. Seth also says evolution has no reason to produce the split, and that keeping it is energetically expensive [spya-ycpfzs].

Seth's point is that if the brain's physical makeup matters to what it does, then digital computation isn't all that counts. That is evidence against computational functionalism, the view that running the right computation is enough for consciousness [spya-p4vmm0].

He supports this with two further points:
- Neurons can't be swapped for perfect silicon equivalents, because some do metabolic work such as clearing waste [spya-un9fjn].
- Brains live in continuous physical time, while an algorithm only has an order of steps [spya-v52g4f].

His other three arguments build on this one. They say that non-algorithmic dynamics may matter [spya-gw0hsq], that life may be necessary for consciousness [spya-hj5y6s], and that simulating something isn't the same as producing it [spya-npjt4j]. He says each can stand alone [spya-nv6tp0]. He also admits he has no knock-down argument and that he could be wrong [spya-qu7j89].

The main argument is that brains are not computers, so the software/hardware split that computational functionalism relies on doesn't exist in them. Seth calls this the "first, and most important" of four arguments [spya-a8jgf4].

Computational functionalism is the claim that running the right algorithm is enough for consciousness [spya-wepmnr]. In a computer, the algorithm is cleanly separate from the physical machine running it, so the same program runs on any suitable hardware. That is the "substrate independence" of Turing computation [spya-dfujdu]. An engineer will recognise it as the usual design principle of abstraction layers.

Seth says the brain has no such layer. Its activity runs across many scales, from large cortical regions down to molecular metabolism, and each neuron is busy keeping itself alive [spya-cf8rt8]. So it is "difficult, and likely impossible" to separate what a brain does from what it is [spya-zw2m7u]. He adds that evolution had no reason to build the separation, and that keeping one is energetically costly [spya-ycpfzs]. If the material matters to the function, then digital computation isn't all that counts [spya-p4vmm0].

Two supports follow from this:
- **Neuron replacement:** you can't swap a neuron for a silicon equivalent with identical function. Some neurons fire partly to clear metabolic waste, which would need a silicon metabolism. This undercuts Chalmers' neural-replacement thought experiment [spya-un9fjn spya-ahtr6e].
- **Time:** an algorithm cares only about the order of steps. Brains work in continuous physical time [spya-v2q8qk spya-v52g4f].

The other three arguments build on this one: non-Turing kinds of computation and dynamics, the role of life, and the gap between simulating something and instantiating it. Seth says each can stand alone [spya-nv6tp0].

My inference is that this is a plausibility argument, not a proof. He gives reasons to doubt the assumption, and he concedes that he might be wrong [spya-qu7j89].

No. The article never mentions global workspace theory by name. It doesn't name any specific theory of consciousness except Searle's biological naturalism and predictive processing, and I searched the text for "global workspace" and found nothing.

The nearest thing is one passage about "other theories of consciousness" in general. Seth says these theories offer accounts "framed in terms of standard computation-as-we-know-it." He adds that they generally avoid proposing sufficient conditions for consciousness and "sidestep defending computational functionalism, being content instead to assume it" [spya-qu7j89]. He then says that doesn't make them wrong, and that nobody can claim to know for sure what it would take to create artificial consciousness, or to avoid creating it [spya-zajp75].

My inference is that global workspace theory is one of the theories he has in mind there, because it is usually stated in terms of information broadcast across a system. The article doesn't say so, and the argument doesn't depend on it. His case is aimed at computational functionalism itself, so it would apply to any theory that rests on that assumption [spya-wepmnr].

Mostly yes, but it's a simplification. The article's line is that consciousness is "the difference between normal wakefulness and the oblivion of deep general anesthesia" [spya-j0a9rq]. It works as a quick pointer to what consciousness means: experience, as opposed to doing. Deep general anaesthesia is a fair example of experience being switched off.

The article doesn't claim more than that, and it isn't a definition of consciousness. The definition it uses is Nagel's "something it is like" to be the organism [spya-j0a9rq]. You'll know better than I do that wakefulness and awareness can separate. The article doesn't say so, but this is from my own background knowledge and I haven't checked it here:

- Dreaming is experience without wakefulness.
- Some patients with open eyes and sleep-wake cycles show no sign of awareness.
- Some patients who can't respond may still have some awareness. Brain-imaging studies of this are well known.
- Sedatives such as ketamine can leave vivid experience in a patient who looks unresponsive.

So "awake versus anaesthetised" is a good first approximation, not a clean on/off line.

My inference is that the bedside picture supports the author's wider argument. If behaviour can be a poor guide to whether anyone is experiencing anything in humans, then a chatbot's fluent output is weak evidence too. The article makes this kind of point when it says there are no definitive tests of machine consciousness [spya-kqs33c] and that intelligence is about doing while consciousness is about being [spya-nj888h].

The article's anaesthesia line works as a pointer, but it is a simplification. It says consciousness is "the difference between normal wakefulness and the oblivion of deep general anesthesia" [spya-j0a9rq]. It uses this as a quick way to show what "something it is like" means. The argument doesn't rest on it, and the article doesn't claim that anaesthesia always switches experience off.

Anaesthesia research suggests it is messier than "oblivion". The isolated forearm technique keeps one arm free of paralysing drugs, so a patient can squeeze a hand on command. [A meta-analysis of 22 studies](https://www.bjanaesthesia.org.uk/article/S0007-0912(18)30130-2/fulltext) found that [393 of 1,131 patients (34.8%) responded at some point](https://core.ac.uk/search?q=Anaesthesia). The studies were of low methodological quality and varied a lot, so treat that figure loosely. Researchers distinguish "connected" consciousness (aware of the surroundings) from "disconnected" consciousness (inner experience such as dreaming, cut off from the surroundings). [Such responses are rarely followed by explicit recall afterwards](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/systems-neuroscience/articles/10.3389/fnsys.2019.00036/full). So deep anaesthesia isn't a reliable on/off switch for experience.

The ICU side matters more for you. Being awake and being conscious can come apart, and so can being unresponsive and being unconscious. In a 2024 NEJM study, [60 of 241 brain-injured patients (25%) who didn't follow commands at the bedside](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC7617195/) still showed command-following on fMRI or EEG. The authors call this cognitive motor dissociation. Absence of outward response doesn't prove absence of experience.

Oddly, this supports the article's wider point. The author says there are [no definitive tests for deciding whether an AI is actually conscious](spya-kqs33c), because there is no agreement on what consciousness requires. Your bedside problem is a milder version of that, since behaviour is an imperfect guide to experience. My inference is that this cuts both ways. Behaviour can under-report consciousness, as in cognitive motor dissociation. It can also over-report it, as with a fluent chatbot. The article stresses the second risk [spya-d89xf7].

Substrate independence is the idea that a computation is the same whatever it runs on, so the same algorithm gives the same result on any machine, much like one program running on different processors [spya-dfujdu]. Seth says the idea is really "substrate flexible", since you can't build a computer out of just any material (cheese won't do) [spya-dfujdu]. He argues that brains don't work this way, because you can't separate what they do from what they are, and that this weakens the case for conscious AI [spya-p4vmm0].

Substrate independence means a computation is the same whatever it runs on: an algorithm does the same thing on any machine, so the software can be separated cleanly from the hardware [spya-dfujdu]. Seth says "substrate flexible" is the better phrase, because you can't build a working computer from just any material, and cheese won't do [spya-dfujdu]. His argument is that brains don't work this way, since what they do can't be separated from what they are, and that this weakens the idea that consciousness is just computation [spya-zw2m7u spya-p4vmm0].

By "simulation" the author means a computer model that reproduces how something behaves without producing the thing itself. He sets it against "instantiation," which means actually bringing the thing into being. "An algorithmic simulation of a continuous process is just that — a simulation, not the process itself" [spya-cepmwf].

His examples: a simulated digestive system digests nothing, and a simulated rainstorm wets nothing. A simulation of X only instantiates X if X is itself a computational process [spya-npjt4j].

Applied to brains, a detailed simulation of a brain would give rise to consciousness only if consciousness is a matter of computation [spya-pbcr03]. The author doubts that. He uses the same point against mind-uploading, saying you're no more likely to exist in a brain simulation than "a hailstorm is likely to arise inside the computers of the U.K. meteorological office" [spya-xvm37k].

He also applies it to Bostrom's simulation hypothesis, which he says quietly assumes that a suitable program would be conscious [spya-xdy4fe].

By simulation, the author means a digital computer's model of a process. It reproduces the process's behavior in symbols and numbers, but not the thing itself. He puts it as "the map" versus "the territory" [spya-cepmwf].

His examples: a simulated digestive system digests nothing, and a simulated rainstorm wets nothing [spya-npjt4j]. Simulations generally lack "the causal powers and intrinsic properties" of what they model. *Instantiation* is the real thing coming into being. A simulation of X instantiates X only if X is itself a computation (an algorithm) [spya-npjt4j].

This is why the point matters for his argument. A detailed simulation of a brain would produce consciousness only if consciousness is a matter of computation, which is the very assumption he doubts [spya-pbcr03]. As an engineer, you may find it easiest to read this as "a model is not the plant."

The article never defines "mythology" outright, so this is my reading from how he uses it. He means a cluster of widely held, mostly unexamined beliefs about AI. They are kept going by psychology, culture and money more than by argument. He uses the word twice in the body: the first piece of that cluster is the "first step in challenging the mythology of conscious AI" [spya-k850tu], and later he mentions "the mythology of ancestor simulations, mind-uploading and the like" [spya-ryg483].

My inference is that the mythology has three layers:

- **Psychological.** Anthropocentrism, human exceptionalism and anthropomorphism lead us to assume intelligence and consciousness come as a package [spya-cvaqgs spya-nxxnrj]. Language makes this worse, as does the habit of calling LLM errors "hallucinations" [spya-t29n67].
- **Cultural and commercial.** He points to the "techno-rapture" and the Promethean pull of playing God [spya-v4sduf]. He also hints that the semi-magical story helps share prices and salaries [spya-mcaa4g].
- **Philosophical.** The load-bearing assumption is computational functionalism: the view that the right computation is enough for consciousness. He says it is "so deeply ingrained that it can be difficult to recognize it as an assumption at all" [spya-wepmnr]. The simulation hypothesis, mind uploading and the "neural replacement" thought experiment all take it for granted [spya-xdy4fe spya-pbcr03].

The ending ties this to religion. He says silicon-rapture fantasies are "a regression to the Cartesian soul" [spya-gvzuc4]. So "mythology" is also meant literally: a secular story of immortality and disembodied rationality.

He doesn't call the belief false. He says conscious AI is "very unlikely" but that he "might be wrong" [spya-c5ve5t spya-qu7j89]. The charge is that the belief is held as inevitable and unexamined, and a position held that way is working as a myth.

The article never defines "mythology" in one sentence. My inference is that it means a bundle of stories we tell ourselves, which feel obvious but rest on unexamined assumptions, and which also serve psychological and commercial interests.

The pieces I can point to:

- **The core assumption.** The "very idea of conscious AI rests on the assumption that consciousness is a matter of computation." Seth calls this computational functionalism, and says it is so ingrained that it is hard to see as an assumption at all [spya-wepmnr]. He later gives Bostrom's simulation argument as an example. Bostrom takes it as given that "a computer running a suitable program would be conscious" [spya-xdy4fe].
- **The psychological pull.** Anthropocentrism, human exceptionalism and anthropomorphism lead us to bundle intelligence with consciousness [spya-cvaqgs]. Seth also names the exponential-curve feeling that we are always on the cusp of a transition [spya-cke6sj]. He compares the whole tendency to pareidolia, seeing a face in toast [spya-k850tu].
- **The religious structure.** He calls the "techno-rapture" a Promethean lure that offers immortality in a silicon cloud [spya-v4sduf]. In his closing section he calls mind-uploading "a regression to the Cartesian soul" [spya-gvzuc4]. So "mythology" is partly meant literally: a secular story with the shape of a salvation myth.
- **The commercial and cultural layer.** He suggests the idea may help share prices stay high [spya-mcaa4g]. He also ties it to "bad science fiction" and tech companies' "self-serving narrative" [spya-hbueqc].

"Mythology" is not a claim that conscious AI is impossible. Seth says nothing he has argued "rules out the possibility of artificial consciousness altogether" [spya-rn8y3y]. He also warns against overconfidence in either direction [spya-zajp75]. The target is the inevitability narrative: the unexamined belief that consciousness comes along as AI gets smarter.

For a philosophy reader, one caution is that "myth" here carries some rhetorical weight. Seth admits that his own biological naturalism is a minority view and that he has no "knock-down argument" [spya-hj5y6s]. The label is aimed at unexamined assumptions, not at functionalism as a position that can be argued for.

The strongest argument, in my judgment, is the first: brains are not computers. The author calls it the "most important" one [spya-a8jgf4], and the other three lean on it.

Its core is that a computer cleanly separates software from hardware, but a brain doesn't. That separation is something humans designed in, following Turing [spya-ycpfzs]. In a brain, "what they do" and "what they are" can't easily be pulled apart [spya-zw2m7u]. Evolution has no obvious reason to pay the energy cost of a clean split [spya-ycpfzs]. The consequence is that if the brain's physical makeup matters to its function, then running the right algorithm on any hardware is not enough for consciousness [spya-p4vmm0]. He backs this with a concrete case: some neurons fire partly to clear metabolic waste, so a silicon stand-in would need its own metabolism [spya-un9fjn]. That undercuts the "replace neurons one by one" thought experiment [spya-ahtr6e].

The simulation argument is logically tidy, but it is conditional. By the author's own account, a simulated brain produces consciousness only if consciousness is computational [spya-pbcr03]. So it adds nothing independent. The "life matters" argument is the most speculative, and he admits he has no knock-down case for it [spya-hj5y6s].

There is a gap in the first argument. My inference is that it shows real brains aren't built like Turing machines. It doesn't show that the consciousness-relevant part couldn't be captured at some level of abstraction. That is the point the other side would press. He concedes his view is a minority one and that he might be wrong [spya-qu7j89].

The case for conscious AI rests on computational functionalism, the assumption that the right computation is enough for consciousness [spya-wepmnr]. That assumption needs a clean split between what a system does (software) and what it is made of (hardware). Seth argues the brain has no such split: its multiscale activity can't be separated from its physical makeup [spya-zw2m7u], and evolution gave no reason to build one [spya-ycpfzs]. The "simulation is not instantiation" argument [spya-npjt4j] is intuitive: a simulated storm gets nothing wet. The "life matters" argument is the weakest, and he admits he has no knock-down case for it [spya-hj5y6s].

The limit of the strongest argument is that it shows computational functionalism is unproven, not that it is false. Seth concedes he might be wrong, and that the other theories of consciousness mostly assume computational functionalism rather than defend it [spya-qu7j89]. The article doesn't blame one person for the myth. It gives the brain-as-computer idea a lineage instead. (My earlier answer cited a malformed id. The thesis is in [spya-wepmnr]: conscious AI assumes consciousness is a matter of computation.)

Seth says "Alan Turing towers above everyone else in this story" [spya-u9egtc]. Turing's definition of computation, built on the abstract Turing machine, is the foundation [spya-cf70dt]. Warren McCulloch and Walter Pitts then showed that networks of simplified neurons can perform logical operations. Stephen Kleene and others showed such networks are "Turing complete" [spya-va8qxr]. Seth calls the union of the two a "mathematical marriage of convenience" [spya-v5vz2t]. Today's artificial neural networks are its "children" [spya-va72zk].

Seth treats these figures as the source of a useful metaphor, not as authors of the myth. He says the metaphor was "extremely productive" [spya-a8jgf4]. The trouble starts when people forget it is a metaphor [spya-uwxe4h].

He points to other contributors as well:
- Human psychological biases: anthropocentrism, human exceptionalism and anthropomorphism [spya-cvaqgs].
- Techno-rapture and tech-industry incentives [spya-v4sduf spya-mcaa4g].
- Named thinkers who take the computational view for granted. These include Chalmers and Hinton (the neural-replacement thought experiment) [spya-ahtr6e] and Nick Bostrom (the simulation hypothesis) [spya-xdy4fe].

The essay doesn't pin the myth on one person. It treats it as a mix of old ideas and human habits.

On the technical side, the brain-as-computer idea traces to Turing's definition of computation, plus McCulloch and Pitts's simplified neurons, which Kleene and others extended [spya-cf70dt spya-va8qxr]. Seth calls the result a "mathematical marriage of convenience" [spya-v5vz2t]. He doesn't blame them, though. He says the metaphor has been "extremely productive" [spya-a8jgf4]. His complaint is that it hardened into an unexamined assumption, which he calls computational functionalism [spya-wepmnr]. Engineers will recognise its core: the clean split between software and hardware.

The essay blames three other things for the myth:
- Built-in biases: anthropocentrism, human exceptionalism and anthropomorphism [spya-cvaqgs].
- The appeal of a "techno-rapture" [spya-v4sduf].
- More cynically, hype that helps share prices [spya-mcaa4g].

He also names people who rely on the assumption without examining it. These include Chalmers and Hinton, through the neural-replacement thought experiment [spya-ahtr6e], and Bostrom, in the simulation hypothesis [spya-xdy4fe].

My earlier one-line summary cited an incomplete block id. The essay's central claim is at [spya-wepmnr].

rows.answer:
The article never gives LLMs a section of their own. It treats them as the main case for its broader argument that intelligence is not consciousness.

**Why LLMs attract the claim.** The author says LLMs like ChatGPT and Claude have been the focus of most of the excitement about artificial consciousness. He thinks this is because language is a cornerstone of human exceptionalism. As a test, he notes that nobody claims DeepMind's AlphaFold is conscious, though it is built much like an LLM. It predicts protein structure rather than words, so it "just doesn't pull our psychological strings in the same way" [spya-k6fpme]. His point is that our reaction tracks language, not anything about the machinery. Three biases drive it: anthropocentrism, human exceptionalism and anthropomorphism [spya-h4mwb2 spya-her4zk].

**Vocabulary.** He objects to saying LLMs "hallucinate". Hallucination is a conscious experience that has lost its grip on reality, so the word quietly credits the system with experience. He prefers "confabulate", which means making things up without realizing it. That is about doing, not experiencing [spya-t29n67].

**What he claims about their status.** He grants that AI systems "can certainly do things", so they are intelligent in some form. Whether there is anything it is like to be ChatGPT is, in his words, "harder to say" [spya-xm96be]. He argues consciousness should not be expected to "come along for the ride" as systems get smarter. Anyone who says it will emerge at the threshold of artificial general intelligence is, he says, showing human exceptionalism [spya-cqh2pq].

**Why he doubts it, as it applies to LLMs.** Today's artificial neural networks descend from the McCulloch-Pitts neuron and run algorithms in the Turing sense [spya-va72zk]. So they depend on computational functionalism. That is the assumption that the right computation is enough for consciousness. He thinks the assumption is shaky, for four reasons:
- Brains are not computers.
- Other kinds of dynamics exist beyond algorithms.
- Life may matter for consciousness.
- Simulating something does not create it [spya-wepmnr spya-cv97j7].

He also takes on Hinton's claim that conscious AI is already here. Hinton leaned on the "neural replacement" thought experiment, and the author says it fails because no perfect silicon stand-in for a biological neuron is possible [spya-ahtr6e].

**Limits of his claim.** He says consciousness is "very unlikely" to arrive with smarter AI, and may be impossible for silicon digital computers. But he adds that "nothing in what I've said rules out" artificial consciousness altogether [spya-c5ve5t spya-rn8y3y]. He concedes his biological-naturalist view is a minority one [spya-qu7j89]. He is more worried about accidental consciousness in brain organoids than in "any new wave of LLM" [spya-vs0vpj].

**The nearer danger: conscious-seeming systems.** He treats LLMs mainly as systems that seem conscious, and he cites Lemoine and Google's LaMDA as the example [spya-cvyfqe spya-p8ky7g]. Such systems raise their own problems. We may grant rights they don't need, or distort our moral concern, or risk "brutalizing our minds" by treating them as feelingless [spya-n0bnf9]. He adds that the feeling may persist even when we know better, like the Müller-Lyer illusion, where the lines look unequal however often you check [spya-xk9gne]. He expects our biases to produce more false positives than false negatives for AI. LLMs resemble us in ways that don't matter for consciousness, such as language, and differ in ways that may matter, such as being alive [spya-d89xf7].

**Why they feel conscious.** Language is the reason LLMs draw so much of the consciousness excitement, because language is "a cornerstone of human exceptionalism." He adds that calling LLM errors "hallucinations" quietly credits them with experience. He prefers "confabulate," which describes making things up, not experiencing [spya-t29n67].

**What they are, in his framework.** He grants that AI is arguably already intelligent in some ways [spya-gjy45p].
